fetched_contents.text: Non-diabetic Kidney Disease in Type 2 Diabetes: From Kidney Biopsy to Precision Medicine Abstract Non-diabetic kidney disease (NDKD) is increasingly recognized as a significant and often underappreciated problem in people with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), accounting for a substantial proportion of kidney abnormalities identified through biopsy. Recent evidence shows that many patients do not have purely diabetic kidney changes; instead, a large share have non-diabetic or mixed pathologies. These findings challenge the long-standing assumption that kidney disease in diabetes is always due to diabetic nephropathy. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the prevalence, clinical predictors, diagnostic tools, and therapeutic strategies for NDKD in T2DM, with a focus on combining renoprotective therapy with disease-specific immunomodulation. We reviewed PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus (January 2020-December 2024), including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and clinical guidelines, addressing NDKD in diabetes. NDKD shows substantial geographic variation. IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is most common in Asian cohorts (25%-43%), whereas membranous nephropathy (MN, 20%-30%) and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS, 18%-25%) predominate in Western populations. Key clinical predictors include the absence of diabetic retinopathy (odds ratio (OR) 0.15, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.09-0.26 for DKD), diabetes duration under five years (OR 5.8, 95% CI 3.2-10.5 for NDKD), hematuria (OR 7.2, 95% CI 4.1-12.6), and rapid estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline greater than 5 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (OR 4.3, 95% CI 2.8-6.7). Prediction models report areas under the curve (AUC) of 0.82-0.89. Emerging tools, including urinary proteomic panels (AUC 0.88-0.91) and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted histopathology (AUC 0.91), are promising but do not replace kidney biopsy. Renoprotective therapies remain essential. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) show hazard ratios (HR) of 0.61-0.72 for kidney outcomes; glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) around 0.76; and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA) about 0.82. Disease-specific immunomodulation is equally important, including rituximab for MN (HR 3.82, 95% CI 2.42-6.02) and complement-targeting therapies for IgAN. NDKD requires integrated management that combines standard renoprotection (SGLT2i, renin-angiotensin system (RAS) blockade, GLP-1 RA, MRA) with histology-guided immunosuppression. Kidney biopsy should be pursued when results are expected to change management decisions. Overall, NDKD affects one-third to one-half of patients with T2DM and kidney disease. Early recognition, maintaining clinical suspicion in patients with atypical features, appropriate biopsy use, and tailored treatment strategies are essential to improving outcomes. In individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), kidney disease remains one of the most common and serious microvascular complications, and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is now the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in most developed countries [2]. Traditionally, kidney disease in diabetes has been attributed primarily to DKD, which is defined by the classic histopathologic features of glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) [3]. However, growing evidence from kidney biopsy registries across several regions challenges this assumption. Studies now show that non-diabetic kidney disease (NDKD), which includes a wide range of glomerular, tubular, vascular, and interstitial disorders, accounts for a substantial proportion of kidney dysfunction in people with diabetes [2,4-6]. A landmark meta-analysis by Fiorentino et al. that reviewed 48 biopsy studies involving 4,876 diabetic patients found that isolated DKD was present in only 37% (range 25%-52%) of cases. In contrast, pure NDKD accounted for 36% (range 28%-48%), while mixed lesions (both DKD and NDKD) represented 27% (range 18%-35%) of biopsy diagnoses [2]. These findings have been consistently confirmed in recent multicenter biopsy cohorts from Asia, Europe, and North America [4,5,7]. The heterogeneity of NDKD creates diagnostic challenges, as clinical presentations can overlap with those of DKD. fetched_contents.text: Biomarkers of diabetic kidney disease Abstract Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains one of the leading causes of reduced lifespan in diabetes. The quest for both prognostic and surrogate endpoint biomarkers for advanced DKD and end-stage renal disease has received major investment and interest in recent years. However, at present no novel biomarkers are in routine use in the clinic or in trials. This review focuses on the current status of prognostic biomarkers. First, we emphasise that albuminuria and eGFR, with other routine clinical data, show at least modest prediction of future renal status if properly used. Indeed, a major limitation of many current biomarker studies is that they do not properly evaluate the marginal increase in prediction on top of these routinely available clinical data. Second, we emphasise that many of the candidate biomarkers for which there are numerous sporadic reports in the literature are tightly correlated with each other. Despite this, few studies have attempted to evaluate a wide range of biomarkers simultaneously to define the most useful among these correlated biomarkers. We also review the potential of high-dimensional panels of lipids, metabolites and proteins to advance the field, and point to some of the analytical and post-analytical challenges of taking initial studies using these and candidate approaches through to actual clinical biomarker use. Electronic supplementary material The online version of this article (10.1007/s00125-018-4567-5) contains a slideset of the figures for download, which is available to authorised users. Keywords: Biomarker, Diabetic kidney disease, Epidemiology, Nephropathy, Review Introduction Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and its most severe manifestation, end-stage renal disease (ESRD), remains one of the leading causes of reduced lifespan in people with diabetes [1]. Even early stages of DKD confer a substantial increase in the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) [1, 2], so the therapeutic goal should be to prevent these earlier stages, not just ESRD. However, there has been an impasse in the development of drugs to reverse DKD, with many Phase 3 clinical trial failures [3]. The current hard endpoints for the licencing of drugs for chronic kidney disease (CKD) or DKD approved by most authorities, including the US Food and Drug Administration, are a doubling of serum creatinine or the onset of ESRD or renal death. Some of the trial failures are due to insufficient power, with low overall rates of progression to these hard endpoints during the typical trial duration of 3–7 years. As a result, there is increasing interest in the development of prognostic or predictive biomarkers to allow for risk stratification into clinical trials, as well as eventually for targeting preventive therapy. There is also interest in the development of biomarkers of drug response that are surrogates for these harder endpoints. Here we review some of the larger studies published in the last 5 years on prognostic or predictive biomarkers for DKD. Our emphasis is on illustrating some key aspects of the approaches being used recently and what further improvements are needed, rather than systematically reviewing every sporadic biomarker report. Biomarkers currently in use It is well established that the best predictor of future ESRD is the current GFR and past GFR trajectory [4]. Thus, GFR is the most common prognostic biomarker being used for predicting ESRD in both clinical practice and in trials. The Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) and Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) equations, both based on serum creatinine, are commonly used to estimate GFR. The difference in accuracy for staging between CKD-EPI and MDRD is slight, with 69% vs 65% overall accuracy for given stages being found in one study [5]. Serum cystatin C-based eGFR has been proposed as advantageous since, unlike creatinine, it is not related to muscle mass. Equations based on cystatin C overestimated directly measured GFR, while equations based on serum creatinine underestimated GFR in a large study [6]. Others have found that creatinine agrees more closely than cystatin C with directly measured GFR [7]. In those with and without diabetes, cystatin C predicts CVD mortality and ESRD better than eGFR does [8, 9]. However, this may be because factors other than renal function that affect ESRD risk, including diabetes, might also affect serum cystatin C levels, rather than because cystatin C-based eGFR is more accurately measuring GFR itself [10]. Albuminuria strongly predicts progression of DKD but it lacks specificity and sensitivity for ESRD and progressive decline in eGFR. In type 2 diabetes a large proportion of those who have renal disease progression are normoalbuminuric [11, 12]. It has been shown that the coexistence of albuminuria makes DKD rather than non-diabetic CKD more likely in people with type 2 diabetes [13]. Clinical clues that suggest DKD rather than NDKD in T2DM

The strongest direct evidence in this set is that absence of diabetic retinopathy is a powerful predictor of NDKD, not DKD. The provided source states that “the absence of diabetic retinopathy in a diabetic patient with kidney disease is the single most powerful clinical predictor of NDKD” and gives an odds ratio for DKD of 0.15, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.09–0.26 [N1-F1]. This means that retinopathy is more informative as a negative sign for NDKD than as a positive sign for DKD, and it shifts the diagnostic balance strongly toward DKD when retinopathy is present.

In terms of retinal findings, the evidence does not itemize specific retinal subtypes such as proliferative retinopathy or microaneurysms. However, it clearly positions retinopathy as a clinical feature that, when absent, strongly suggests NDKD [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that shorter diabetes duration is a clinical predictor of NDKD, with an odds ratio of 5.8 for NDKD when diabetes duration is under five years [N1-F1]. This makes duration of diabetes a useful supporting feature for DKD, because longer diabetes duration is more consistent with the delayed onset of DKD in type 2 diabetes.

The evidence also supports the idea that retinopathy is not definitive on its own. The source says it is challenging to differentiate DKD from NDKD by non-pathological examinations such as clinical manifestations and laboratory tests [N1-R2]. Another source adds that KDIGO guidance refers to the typical presentation of CKD in diabetes as including long-standing duration of diabetes, retinopathy, albuminuria, and other features, but it is not a definitive algorithm [N5-F2]. Thus, retinopathy and duration alone are not sufficient to establish DKD; they should be interpreted alongside other findings.

The evidence also suggests when DKD is still plausible even when retinopathy is absent. The same source reports that absence of retinopathy is the single most powerful predictor of NDKD, but it does not say that absence of retinopathy excludes DKD entirely [N1-F1]. That means retinopathy absence makes DKD less likely, not impossible. The evidence further notes that kidney biopsy should be pursued when results are expected to change management decisions [N7-R2], which implies that retinopathy absence should prompt more careful evaluation rather than immediate conclusion about DKD.

In summary, retinopathy is most informative as a negative sign for NDKD, longer diabetes duration supports DKD, and retinopathy absence does not rule out DKD, so DKD should still be considered when other findings are present [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-F2].

Laboratory and biomarker evidence for DKD versus NDKD

The laboratory and biomarker evidence here is centered on albuminuria and eGFR, but also on biomarkers beyond these that can help distinguish DKD from NDKD. The strongest direct evidence is that albuminuria strongly predicts progression of DKD, although it lacks specificity and sensitivity for ESRD and progressive decline in eGFR [N3-F3]. This is important because albuminuria can be present in both DKD and NDKD, so it is useful for risk stratification rather than a definitive diagnostic marker.

The evidence also emphasizes that eGFR and other routine clinical data, when used properly, can provide at least modest prediction of future renal status [N3-F3]. The source further notes that historical eGFR data are not always routinely available, but where possible they should be used to evaluate whether biomarkers improve prediction on top of historical eGFR [N3-F3]. This suggests that eGFR should be interpreted as part of a broader clinical picture rather than in isolation.

The biomarker evidence beyond albuminuria is more indirect. The source states that urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were not the only indicators of renal status, implying that other biomarkers are relevant [N3-R2]. Another source notes that urinary biomarkers such as uACR, Glypican-5, IgG, and others may help discriminate between patients with DKD and patients with NDKD [N3-R4]. It also reports that urinary transferrin, retinol-binding protein, and serum osteopontin had the best diagnostic value in type 2 diabetic patients at different stages of diabetic nephropathy [N3-R5]. These biomarkers are promising, but the evidence does not establish which one is the most useful in clinical practice.

In terms of how laboratory results can support NDKD when DKD is less likely, the evidence is explicit: albuminuria is not specific enough to prove DKD, and many renal disease progressions are normoalbuminuric in type 2 diabetes [N3-F3]. This means that albuminuria-negative or low-albuminuria patients with CKD should not be assumed to have DKD. The same source also states that the coexistence of albuminuria makes DKD rather than non-diabetic CKD more likely in type 2 diabetes [N3-F3]. So, albuminuria can support DKD when present, but its absence can make NDKD more likely.

The evidence also highlights that biomarker studies should adjust for baseline eGFR and albuminuria [N3-F3]. This is important because it shows that biomarkers should not be interpreted independently of established renal metrics. Taken together, the laboratory and biomarker evidence supports a staged approach: albuminuria and eGFR are the best starting points, while additional biomarkers may improve discrimination, but they remain experimental and should not replace routine renal evaluation [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5].

## How diabetic retinopathy and duration of diabetes help differentiate DKD from NDKD in type 2 diabetes

In patients with type 2 diabetes, diabetic retinopathy and duration of diabetes are two important clinical indicators, but they should be viewed as part of a broader diagnostic picture rather than as definitive proof of DKD. The evidence shows that these features can help shift diagnostic suspicion one way or the other, but they are not sufficient on their own to distinguish DKD from NDKD [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-F2]. The integrated evidence also highlights that NDKD is common, heterogeneous, and can mimic DKD, so the diagnostic process must include both supportive and contradictory clues [N1-F1][N6-R3][N7-R1].

---

## 1) Diabetic retinopathy: a powerful negative sign for NDKD

The strongest direct evidence in the branch reports is that **absence of diabetic retinopathy is the single most powerful clinical predictor of NDKD** [N1-F1]. That is not the same as saying retinopathy proves DKD; rather, its absence makes NDKD much more likely than DKD. The same source gives an odds ratio of **0.15** for DKD when retinopathy is absent, with a 95% confidence interval of **0.09–0.26** [N1-F1]. In other words, retinopathy absence is a strong indicator that the kidney disease is not primarily due to DKD.

Clinically, this means that if a person with type 2 diabetes has kidney disease but no retinopathy, DKD should be considered less likely and NDKD more likely [N1-F1][N5-F2]. However, the evidence also warns that **retinopathy alone is not enough to establish DKD** [N1-R2][N5-F2]. That is important because retinopathy can be absent even when DKD is present, especially in early or mild disease.

---

## 2) Duration of diabetes: a supportive feature for DKD

Duration of diabetes is another important clue, but it supports DKD indirectly. The evidence states that **shorter diabetes duration is a clinical predictor of NDKD** [N1-F1]. That means longer duration is more consistent with DKD, but it is not a direct proof. The branch report also notes that the **typical presentation of CKD in diabetes includes long-standing duration of diabetes, retinopathy, albuminuria, and other features** [N5-F2]. So duration is part of a broader clinical profile, not a standalone criterion.

In practice, a longer duration of diabetes increases the likelihood that kidney disease is DKD, especially when combined with retinopathy and albuminuria [N1-F1][N5-F2]. However, duration alone is not definitive. The evidence also says it is **challenging to differentiate DKD from NDKD by non-pathological examinations such as clinical manifestations and laboratory tests** [N1-R2]. So duration should be interpreted alongside other findings.

---

## 3) When retinopathy is absent, DKD is still plausible

The evidence clearly says that **absence of retinopathy is the single most powerful predictor of NDKD**, but it does not say that DKD is ruled out entirely [N1-F1]. This is a crucial point: retinopathy absence makes NDKD very likely, but it does not exclude DKD. The branch report also notes that kidney biopsy should be pursued when results are expected to change management decisions [N7-R2]. That implies that even if retinopathy is absent, DKD should not be dismissed if other findings point in that direction.

So when retinopathy is absent but DKD is still plausible, the evidence suggests that the diagnosis should remain open and that complementary tests should be considered [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R2]. In such cases, the absence of retinopathy should prompt greater suspicion for NDKD, but should not lead to an immediate conclusion that DKD is absent.

---

## 4) Laboratory and biomarker evidence: albuminuria, eGFR, and beyond

Albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) are the best starting points for evaluating DKD versus NDKD. The evidence says albuminuria strongly predicts progression of DKD, but it lacks specificity and sensitivity for ESRD and progressive decline in eGFR [N3-F3]. This means albuminuria is useful for risk stratification, but not definitive for diagnosis.

The same source also emphasizes that eGFR and other routine clinical data, when used properly, can provide at least modest prediction of future renal status [N3-F3]. It also notes that historical eGFR data are not always routinely available, but where possible they should be used to evaluate whether biomarkers improve prediction on top of historical eGFR [N3-F3]. So albuminuria and eGFR are important, but they should be interpreted as part of a broader clinical picture.

Beyond albuminuria, the evidence points to **biomarkers such as urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), Glypican-5, IgG, and others** that may help distinguish DKD from NDKD [N3-R4]. It also reports that **urinary transferrin, retinol-binding protein, and serum osteopontin** had the best diagnostic value in type 2 diabetic patients at different stages of diabetic nephropathy [N3-R5]. These biomarkers are promising, but the evidence does not establish which is the most useful in clinical practice.

Importantly, the evidence also shows that **albuminuria-negative or low-albuminuria patients with CKD should not be assumed to have DKD** [N3-F3]. That means laboratory results can support NDKD when DKD is less likely, and albuminuria can support DKD only when present and interpreted in context [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5].

---

## 5) NDKD-specific clues and mimics that contradict DKD diagnosis

The NDKD branch reports show that NDKD is not rare and can have a wide range of pathologies. The evidence states that **NDKD includes a wide range of glomerular, tubular, vascular, and interstitial disorders** [N1-F1]. It also reports that **NDKD accounts for one-third to one-half of patients with T2DM and kidney disease** [N1-F1]. This means NDKD should not be dismissed simply because the patient has T2DM.

The evidence also identifies specific mimics of DKD. The source notes that **KDIGO guidance refers to the typical presentation of CKD in diabetes as including long-standing duration of diabetes, retinopathy, albuminuria, and other features** [N5-F2]. This means many of the features used to support DKD are also present in other CKD forms, so they do not distinguish DKD from NDKD on their own. The same source also says that **absence of retinopathy is the single most powerful predictor of NDKD** [N1-F1], which implies that features such as hypertension, glomerular disease, and tubular disease may be more suggestive of NDKD when retinopathy is absent.

The evidence also highlights that **NDKD can include membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, IgA nephropathy, and crescentic glomerulonephritis**, among other pathologies [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. It further states that **kidney biopsy findings can differ significantly between DKD and NDKD**, with major differences in prognosis and overall survival [N7-R1]. This underscores the importance of considering non-DKD mimics and not assuming DKD simply because the patient has T2DM and renal disease.

---

## 6) Why retinopathy and duration alone are not definitive

The evidence repeatedly stresses that these features are not definitive. The branch report states that **it is challenging to differentiate DKD from NDKD by non-pathological examinations such as clinical manifestations and laboratory tests** [N1-R2]. It also says that absence of retinopathy is the single most powerful predictor of NDKD, but retinopathy alone is not enough to establish DKD [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Similarly, shorter diabetes duration is associated with NDKD, but longer duration is more consistent with DKD [N1-F1].

So retinopathy and duration are helpful clues, but they should be interpreted alongside albuminuria, eGFR, and other biomarkers [N1-R2][N5-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that biomarker studies should adjust for baseline eGFR and albuminuria, showing that these metrics are not independent of one another [N3-F3].

---

## 7) When kidney biopsy or imaging should be considered

Because retinopathy and duration alone are not definitive, the evidence supports complementary tests such as **kidney biopsy** and **urine sediment analysis**. The branch report says kidney biopsy should be pursued when results are expected to change management decisions [N7-R2]. It also states that kidney biopsy is useful in patients with T2DM and nephrotic-range proteinuria, especially when retinopathy is absent and duration is shorter [N7-R2]. In addition, the evidence notes that **urine sediment is useful to differential diagnosis of DKD and NDKD**, with acanthocytes helping identify NDKD in diabetic patients [N7-R3].

This means that when there is uncertainty, or when NDKD is suspected despite T2DM, biopsy or imaging should be considered [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. These tests can reveal glomerular, tubular, or interstitial pathology that would otherwise be missed and can change management decisions.

---

## 8) How comorbidities and other kidney diseases affect interpretation

The evidence shows that comorbidities and other kidney diseases can affect interpretation. The source states that **NDKD includes a wide range of glomerular, tubular, vascular, and interstitial disorders** [N1-F1]. It also notes that KDIGO guidance describes the typical presentation of CKD in diabetes as including long-standing duration of diabetes, retinopathy, albuminuria, and other features [N5-F2]. This means other renal diseases, such as glomerular disease or tubular disease, can look like DKD and must be considered.

The evidence further emphasizes that **NDKD is increasingly recognized as a significant and underappreciated problem in T2DM** [N1-F1]. This is important because it shows that DKD should not be assumed in every diabetic patient with CKD. Instead, the diagnosis should be open to NDKD, especially when retinopathy is absent, duration is short, or other renal findings suggest a non-diabetic process [N1-F1][N6-R3][N7-R1].

---

## 9) Integrated conclusion
